newsitem.title: TURKEY: Turkish shares lifted by "Islamist-free" govt hope.
newsitem.headline: Turkish shares lifted by "Islamist-free" govt hope.

text.p: Hopes of an "Islamist-free" Turkish government being formed fuelled strong gains in Istanbul shares on Friday, brokers said.
A slightly firmer Turkish lira and falling bond yields also reflected a mood of cautious optimism going into the weekend.

President Suleyman Demirel invited opposition leader Mesut Yilmaz for talks, prompting speculation he would be asked to form a coalition to replace the Islamist-led coalition of outgoing leader Necmettin Erbakan.

The IMKB National-100 index leapt on the news and closed up 2.56 percent, or 41 points, at 1,642, after slipping back from a mid-session high of 1,647 following the announcement of Demirel's invitation.
The news sparked a surge in trading volume, which leapt to 27.1 trillion lira ($186 million) from 17.8 trillion a day earlier, when shares gained over two percent.

"Demirel's invitation to Yilmaz prompted a sharp rise," said Levent Yakar from Global Securities. "The market is indexed to politics and may either continue its upward move or retreat, based on solid developments to emerge in Ankara."
Political uncertainty has blighted the volatile financial markets in recent weeks. Shares declined five percent last week.
The Turkish lira, supported by central bank intervention on Wednesday, showed a firmer tone with a marginal rise to 145,870 to the dollar from 145,900 on Wednesday.
In the bond market, yields extended Thursday's declines and eased to 104.5-105 percent from the previous day's close of 106-106.5 percent.

The pro-market Motherland Party leader Yilmaz is one of the favourites to be appointed prime minister-designate following Erbakan's resignation on Wednesday under pressure from the secularist establishment.

"The market bought on expectations that Mesut Yilmaz would be asked to set up a new government. It is obvious that the market will welcome such a development if it becomes true," said Cem Baycan from Delta Securities.
Former prime minister Yilmaz, who has vowed to exclude the Islamists from any coalition, could have trouble finding the parliamentary majority needed to seal any government.

On paper, Yilmaz's arch rival Tansu Ciller has the support of 282 deputies in the 550-seat parliament. Yilmaz has only 129 MPs and would need to win the backing of leftist parties and some dissidents in Ciller's party to pass a confidence vote.
Stock market gains spread during the afternoon from largely state-owned stocks to all sectors and was only offset by a late wave of profit-taking.
Trading was especially heavy in state oil refiner Tupras, steel maker Eregli and utility Cukurova Elektrik.
"The buying which began in public shares in particular has spread across the board," said broker Hasan Soydan of Garanti Securities.
Strong performances from shares in the metals index, which rose more than seven percent, and the transport sector, which was up six percent, boosted the wider market.
Shares in insurers were among the few losers.
